summary:
We developed HYGEIA, a health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts understand their health and act on it during space missions. A wearable, a wrist actigraph, a dosimeter and cabin sensors send readings automatically. HYGEIA compares each one with NASA-STD-3001 limits and the astronaut’s own baseline, then answers three questions: How am I? Why? What do I do now?

It addresses the challenge by tracking the six suggested indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep and mood), plus radiation, exercise, blood oxygen and cabin air. It gives clear guidance and sends reports to the ground automatically, even after a lost link. It adapts to spacecraft, space station, rover and Moon or Mars bases, checks whether each task of the day, such as a spacewalk, is safe, and asks the ground for approval. A crew view shows patterns across astronauts, while health data stays private.

This matters because on deep-space missions, Earth may be minutes away. Crews need to catch small problems early and decide safely on their own. HYGEIA guides; it does not diagnose. The flight surgeon stays in charge.
details:
What it does and how it works
HYGEIA is a health monitoring prototype for astronauts on long missions. It turns automatic health readings into a clear status, a reason and one action the astronaut can follow. Every screen answers three questions: How am I? Why? What do I do now?

A wearable, a wrist actigraph, a personal dosimeter and cabin sensors feed the software on their own (simulated in the prototype). Only blood glucose and mood come from a short daily questionnaire. HYGEIA tracks the six indicators suggested by the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood), plus exercise, radiation, blood oxygen and cabin air.

Each reading follows a traceable chain: indicator → rule → guidance → report to the ground. The reading is compared with NASA-STD-3001 limits and with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline. The level (Normal, Caution, Alert, Critical or No data) is shown with color, an icon and text. Heart rate and blood pressure only change level if they stay out of range for a full time window, so a single odd value does not raise an alarm. Critical values are confirmed within seconds.

The astronaut can act on each piece of guidance: notify the crew medical officer, with an optional note (“noise in the module kept me awake”), or mark it as done. HYGEIA also checks each task of the day, such as a spacewalk, against the indicators that matter for it. It proposes ranked options, like “postpone” or “work in pairs”, each with its reason and expected effect, and asks the ground for approval. Without a link, stricter local rules apply, and spacewalks are never approved without the ground or the crew medical officer. Reports go to the ground automatically through a priority queue that keeps them safe and resends them when the link returns.

Benefits

  • Astronauts understand their health without medical training and know what to do next.
  • No typing, so there are no typing errors, and very little time is taken from the mission.
  • It keeps working when Earth is minutes away or the link is down.
  • The flight surgeon gets complete, structured reports with possible causes listed as hypotheses to confirm, plus the astronaut’s own notes.
  • A crew view spots shared causes: the same signal in two or more people points to the cabin air, light, noise or workload, not to each person.
  • Health data is private by role. The mission team only sees whether each task is approved, never the health numbers.

Intended impact
As missions move to the Moon and Mars, crews will need more autonomy in health care. HYGEIA aims to make that autonomy safe. It helps astronauts act early on small changes before they become emergencies, keeps the medical team informed despite communication delays, and supports decisions about risky tasks. It guides; it does not diagnose. The flight surgeon stays in charge.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Prototype: a single-page web app in HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks and no server. It runs in any modern browser, on desktop and mobile.
  • Fonts: IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono and Barlow Semi Condensed (Google Fonts, open licenses).
  • Testing: automated browser tests with Playwright, covering the demo scenarios on every tab, layout on desktop and mobile screens, the sustained-alert logic and the astronaut’s actions.
  • Hardware: none yet. All devices are simulated with realistic data. The design is based on real devices described by NASA and partner agencies, such as the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor shirt, personal dosimeters, and a Brazilian wrist actigraph flown on Artemis II.
  • Data and standards: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev. C and Vol. 2 Rev. E, NASA Human Research Program risk pages and evidence reports, NASA technical reports on cardiovascular changes, the American Heart Association blood pressure categories, and the Brazilian Diabetes Society glucose guidance.
  • AI use: an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) helped organize the documents, find and check sources, write and test the code, and translate the material into English. The idea, the features and every design decision came from the team. The prototype states this in its footer and HTML metadata.

Creativity

  • Explains, not just measures. Most health tools show numbers; HYGEIA always shows the reason and the action.
  • Mission-aware. The environment (spacecraft, station, rover, Moon or Mars base) changes the limits, the tasks, the risks and the communication delay. For example, the minimum aerobic capacity for a spacewalk rises on a planetary surface.
  • Gravity changes. After landing or arriving on a surface, HYGEIA flags an adaptation period and watches blood pressure and blood oxygen more closely. This is based on NASA data showing that many astronauts struggle to stand on landing day. A guided daily stand test is designed as the next step.
  • Health linked to the schedule. Each task is approved or put on hold based on the astronaut’s health, with ranked alternatives.
  • Crew-level patterns. It looks at the whole crew to find environmental causes.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety: conservative guidance, no diagnosis, and ground guidance always overrides local guidance. Alert and critical reports go out automatically, because an unwell astronaut may not be able to send them.
  • Alarm fatigue: heart rate and blood pressure must stay out of range for a full window before an alert. Next steps include a plausibility check for loose sensors.
  • Data quality: “No data” is never shown as “all good”, and wearable blood pressure is labeled as an estimate to confirm with a direct measurement. Weekly cuff calibration is part of the design.
  • Communication: delay per environment, deadlines for ground replies, and a priority queue that survives link loss. The design calls for a signed, encrypted link following the CCSDS Space Data Link Security standard.
  • Privacy: role-based access, as at NASA, where health data stays with the flight surgeon.
  • Usability: large buttons for gloved hands, color always paired with an icon and text, short plain-language messages, and a mobile layout with bottom navigation.
  • Honesty about limits: clinical ranges other than blood pressure and glucose are marked provisional until validated by physicians, and real use would require clinical validation.
